script_v1_5:
[CH01 | 0:00–0:22 | flashforward_teaser]

In 1674, workmen beneath the Tower stairs uncovered a wooden chest holding two small skeletons. They were called the missing princes almost at once, before the find was properly recorded.

In 1933, anatomists opened the urn and found a jumble of human and animal bone. Their report treated the remains as the princes from the start. For ninety years the findings have remained sealed in Westminster Abbey, leaving one question open: whose bones were they?

[CH02 | 0:22–0:37 | channel_intro_cta]

If you're here for history's darkest mysteries—the ones they don't want solved—hit that like button.

The question is why the evidence stays closed to examination.

To answer that, I'll trace the evidence from 1483 to today, follow the three suspects, and show why the only test that could settle it has stayed blocked for ninety years. Let's go back to where it started.

[CH03 | 0:37–2:42 | victim_ordinary_world]

June 16, 1483.

Two boys, ages twelve and nine, arrived at the Tower of London to await a coronation. The older one, Edward V, had just inherited the throne. His father, Edward IV, had died suddenly two months earlier, leaving the kingdom to a child.

The younger brother, Richard, Duke of York, had been living in sanctuary with their mother at Westminster Abbey. Sanctuary meant church protection—no one could take you by force. But on June 16, the boy's uncle convinced their mother to release him. The brothers should be together, he said. The coronation was coming. The Tower was where kings stayed before their crowning.

Richard joined Edward in the royal apartments. Their uncle, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, had been named Lord Protector. He governed England until Edward turned old enough to rule alone. Parliament had confirmed it. The nobility accepted it. The boys trusted him.

Then Parliament declared that Edward IV's marriage to the boys' mother had never been legal. The reasoning: Edward IV had been secretly pre-contracted to another woman before the wedding. Under church law, that made the marriage invalid.

The two boys were no longer legitimate heirs. Edward V was no longer king. Richard of York was no longer a duke. They lost their claim to the throne, and in an instant they became obstacles to the man who had been named their protector.

Their uncle, the Lord Protector, became King Richard III.

The coronation went ahead on July 6, 1483. But it wasn't Edward's. It was their uncle's.

The two brothers stayed in the Tower.

What happened to them next, only one man wrote down—and his manuscript wouldn't be found for 450 years.

[CH04 | 2:42–4:30 | discovery_scene]

The Tower of London became their world. Two brothers, locked in a medieval fortress while their uncle claimed the crown.

By summer of 1483, an Italian friar named Domenico Mancini was in London on a diplomatic mission. He watched the Tower. He kept notes. What he wrote would become the closest thing we have to what actually happened. In the beginning, they were visible—Edward and Richard, standing at the windows behind the iron bars that looked out onto the courtyard.

Then something changed.

The friar recorded the shift with precision. The boys were withdrawn deeper into the Tower's interior chambers. The windows where they'd been seen went dark. Day after day, fewer appearances. The pattern was unmistakable.

Then nothing.

He watched the windows go empty and stay empty. The boys who had been there—visible, real, alive—simply stopped appearing. Mancini saw it happen in increments. The absence building one day at a time.

But here's what matters about what Mancini wrote. He didn't claim certainty. He didn't say he knew they were dead. What he actually wrote: "There is a common report that they have been done away with. Whether they have been murdered, and by what manner of death, so far I have not at all ascertained."

He saw them vanish. He heard the rumors. But he admitted he had no proof. He could not confirm what had happened. He could not determine how.

That manuscript wasn't discovered until 1934. Four hundred and fifty-one years later.

So if the only eyewitness couldn't confirm what happened—where does the murder story come from?

[CH05 | 4:30–7:25 | crime_scene_walkthrough]

So if Mancini couldn't confirm what happened—where does the murder story actually come from?

If no one who was there wrote down "murder"—who did, and when?

Here's what we have from 1483.

In 1483 there is no direct evidence. By 1486 there is a rumor. Thirty years later Thomas More supplies a complete narrative, but no original document records Tyrrell’s confession.

Around spring 1486, someone continued the Crowland Chronicle—probably a member of Richard III's own council—and wrote: "A rumor was spread that the sons of King Edward had died a violent death, but it was uncertain how."

A rumor. Uncertain how.

Robert Ricart, town clerk of Bristol, kept annual records. His entry for the year ending September 1483 says: "This year, the two sons of King Edward were put to silence in the Tower of London."

Put to silence. Not murdered. Not killed. Silenced.

No method. No accused. No date.

Those are the only two pieces of evidence written while people who might have known something were still alive. Neither says what happened. Neither names a killer. One says rumor. The other says silenced.

Now, there is a detailed account of how the princes died. Two men sent at midnight. Smothered with a featherbed and pillows. Buried at the foot of the stairs. That version comes from Thomas More's History of King Richard III, written around 1513 to 1518.

More names the killer: James Tyrrell, a knight in Richard's service. He says Tyrrell confessed before he died. He says Tyrrell's men entered the chamber while the boys slept, pressed the bedding over their faces until they stopped breathing, then carried the bodies down and buried them under a staircase.

It's vivid. It's complete. It's the story everyone knows.

But More began writing around 1513, thirty years after the princes vanished and twenty-eight years after Richard III died at Bosworth. The supposed killers were all dead. No one More named could confirm or deny what he wrote.

And here's the thing about that confession. Tyrrell was executed on May 6, 1502, for treason—not for murdering the princes. The idea that he confessed to the murders before his death only appears in More's account and in later writers who copied More. There is no original confession document. No trial transcript. No recorded statement from 1502.

The only evidence that Tyrrell ever admitted to anything is a story written by someone else, a decade later, under a king who needed Richard III to be guilty.

The full narrative—the midnight intrusion, the smothering, the burial, the confession—all of that was written thirty years after the princes disappeared by someone working for the dynasty that had defeated Richard and taken his throne.

Every detailed account of the murder comes from after the accused was dead and couldn't defend himself.

[CH06 | 7:25–8:05 | sponsor_message]

Before we go further, I want to tell you about something we've just launched.

We've put together a limited-edition collection based on cases like this one—historical mysteries that never got the investigation they deserved.

It's called the Unsolved Archive. Prints, field notes, reference materials designed for people who care about how evidence works.

Check it out at the link in the description.

All right, back to the Tower.

By the time the bones were placed in Westminster Abbey, a story had already been written. The question is whether anyone was allowed to check if that story was true.

[CH07 | 8:05–10:20 | motive_elimination_suspect_profiling]

On July 17, 1674, King Charles II ordered the demolition of an exterior staircase on the south side of the White Tower at the Tower of London.

Workers were digging about ten feet into the foundation when they hit something that wasn't stone.

A wooden chest. Elm wood.

Inside were two small skeletons.

The royal physician, John Knight, recorded what else was in there: fragments of cloth and pieces of velvet.

That's the find.

No other documentation. No systematic record of exactly where the chest was positioned, how deep the workers had gone, or what condition the bones were in when they came out.

The bones were declared to be the Princes almost immediately.

The reasoning? They were found under a staircase.

Thomas More's account, written thirty years after the alleged murders, had said the bodies were buried at the foot of a staircase in the Tower.

So: staircase, bones, therefore princes.

Except that's circular reasoning. The only evidence the bones belonged to the princes was that they matched a story written 160 years after the bones were buried—a story with no eyewitness sources. They used More's account to identify the bones, then used the bones to confirm More's account.

Except More also wrote that a priest later moved the bodies to a more appropriate location. And historians have pointed out that the staircase where the chest was found probably didn't even exist during Richard III's reign. It was built later.

The one piece of physical evidence used to identify the bones—the location—doesn't match the only detailed account of the murder.

In 1678, Charles II commissioned Christopher Wren to design a marble urn. The bones were placed inside and buried in Westminster Abbey, in the chapel of Henry VII.

The Latin inscription on the urn doesn't say "believed to be" or "thought to be." It reads, in effect: Here lie the bones of Edward V and Richard, Duke of York.

Direct identification. No hedging. No uncertainty.

The urn is still there.

The bones were never examined in any modern sense. No one checked their age using scientific methods available even at that time. No one measured them in detail. No one attempted to verify whether they were male or female.

They were placed in an urn and declared to be the princes because that's what the story required.

And for the next two hundred and fifty-five years, no one was allowed to check whether the story was true.

Until 1933. When someone finally opened the urn—and found something that didn't add up.

[CH08 | 10:20–12:50 | suspect_interview_behavioral_read]

Until 1933.

In 1933, Westminster Abbey archivist Lawrence Tanner opened the urn. With him were anatomist William Wright and dental surgeon George Northcroft.

They had been asked to examine the bones and determine whether they matched the ages of the missing princes.

The examination was completed on July 6, 1933.

Their conclusion: the bones belonged to two children, one approximately twelve to thirteen years old, the other nine to eleven. The ages, they said, were consistent with the princes at the time of their disappearance.

The report was published. The case, it seemed, was closed.

Except the examination had started with the answer already decided.

The investigators were told from the beginning that these were the bones of the princes. They were not asked to determine identity. They were asked to confirm it.

They looked for signs of suffocation because the Tudor narrative said the boys were smothered. They examined the skulls for blood stains, which they interpreted as evidence of asphyxiation.

They did not attempt to determine the sex of the skeletons.

They did not use any of the dating methods available at the time. They relied entirely on visual estimates of age based on tooth development and bone size.

The brief shaped the result: the examiners were asked to match the bones to the princes, not to establish identity from scratch. With the urn already inscribed and the Tudor account already fixed, the 1933 report had little room for an open question.

The bones themselves were in terrible condition. Incomplete. Mixed with animal bones, chicken bones, scattered fragments that clearly did not belong to any human child.

The blood stain interpretation? Rejected by later forensic specialists. Blood does not leave visible stains on bone in that manner after centuries.

The dental evidence? The report claimed that congenital missing teeth and unusual skull sutures indicated close royal inbreeding, proof of Plantagenet blood. Later dental experts pointed out that these traits appear in the general population and prove nothing about lineage.

Wilton M. Krogman, a physical anthropologist at the University of Pennsylvania, reviewed the 1933 findings decades later. His assessment: "These bones cannot be positively and unequivocally identified as those of the princes."

The examination that was supposed to settle the question had been designed to confirm a foregone conclusion. It checked for evidence that fit the Tudor story. It ignored evidence that did not.

And because the bones were returned to the urn immediately after, sealed again in Westminster Abbey, no one has been able to verify or challenge those findings since.

For ninety years. From 1933 to today.

[CH09 | 12:50–15:50 | crime_scene_revisit_entry_reveal]

So if the 1933 examination couldn't settle it, and no one's been allowed to check the findings since—what are we supposed to believe?

Let me show you three pieces of evidence that prove this isn't about technology. It's about choice.

First: public demand exists, and it's been silenced.

In 2013, British citizens petitioned the UK government. They wanted the same thing: open the urn, run modern tests, let science answer what 1933 couldn't. A straightforward request. DNA analysis. The same technology that had already worked on other historical remains. Give the bones a chance to speak for themselves.

The petition was closed. Not rejected after review—closed because it didn't reach the signature threshold to force a parliamentary response.

Westminster Abbey declined. The royal household declined. The academic consensus said nothing.

Historian A.J. Pollard, who's written extensively on Richard III and the princes, made a crucial point: even if DNA confirmed the bones belonged to the boys, it wouldn't prove who killed them. The science could answer identity. It couldn't answer guilt.

The urn is not protected by an unbreakable lock; it is protected by a decision renewed for ninety years. Each year the remains stay sealed, the central evidence remains untested.

[CH10 | 15:50–18:00 | suspect_alibi_verification]

Third—and this is the one that makes the refusal impossible to ignore—they've already done it for someone else.

In 2012, archaeologists excavating a Leicester car park—formerly the site of Greyfriars Church—found a king. They found him.

A male skeleton, age thirty to thirty-four, severe scoliosis of the spine, multiple traumatic injuries to the skull consistent with battlefield weapons. The location matched historical records. The physical description matched contemporary accounts of Richard III's appearance and war wounds.

But matching isn't proof.

On February 5, 2013, the University of Leicester announced the results of mitochondrial DNA analysis. They'd compared the skeleton's DNA to living maternal-line descendants of Richard III's sister. The match probability: 99.999 percent.

It was Richard III. No doubt. Five centuries in the ground, and modern science gave him back his name.

In 2015, his remains were reinterred at Leicester Cathedral in a ceremony attended by thousands. The coffin, the tomb, the location—all open to the public. You can visit him today.

Richard III, the accused. The king historians spent five hundred years calling a child murderer. His bones were dug up from a parking lot, tested with the most rigorous forensic science available, and given a state burial with full transparency.

The two princes—the alleged victims, whose murder defined his reign in every history book—remain in Westminster Abbey. Untested. Unexamined. Protected from the same science that proved who their uncle was.

Both cases involve remains roughly five centuries old, and both could be examined with the same forensic methods. Richard III’s identity was answered by DNA; the princes’ remains are still protected from that test.

The accused killer was given the full dignity of modern science. The alleged victims were locked behind a refusal that no one will explain.

That's not a limitation. That's a choice.

[CH11 | 18:00–19:30 | suspect_timeline_gap_flag]

But there's another problem the bone evidence doesn't solve.

In 1789, workers repairing St. George's Chapel in Windsor Castle opened the tomb of Edward IV and his wife. Next to their vault, they found a small side chamber. Inside were two child-sized coffins. No identification. No records of who was buried there. They sealed it back up and moved on.

Between 1810 and 1813, the chapel was renovated again. This time, in a different location inside the same building, workers found two lead coffins with names on them: George Plantagenet and Mary Plantagenet—two of Edward IV's children who died young, well documented in court records.

Which meant the two coffins found in 1789 were not those two. They were someone else. Two children. Identity unknown. In the same chapel. In the same vault complex as Edward IV himself. Never opened. Never examined.

St. George's Chapel, Windsor, maintains a public webpage about its royal burials. The official statement reads: "The final resting place of the Princes remains unknown."

Not "we believe" they're in Westminster. Not "they were probably moved." Unknown.

The Westminster urn and the Windsor coffins are two separate sets of remains that could be examined. Neither has been opened to modern forensic testing, so both questions remain open.

[CH12 | 19:30–21:15 | red_herring_interrogation]

But there was one more twist. One more person who claimed to know the truth.

In November 1491, a seventeen-year-old Flemish boy walked into Cork, Ireland, and said his name was Richard, Duke of York. The younger brother. The one who vanished from the Tower eight years earlier.

He had the face for it. Contemporary accounts describe him as bearing a striking resemblance to Edward IV. More than that: he knew things. Intimate details about court protocol, family dynamics, the layout of palaces.

He had backing. Edward IV's own sister took him in, funding his claim. The Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I recognized him. The French King Charles VIII recognized him. The Scottish King James IV recognized him. By 1494, Maximilian formally recognized this boy as Richard IV, the rightful King of England.

For seven years, this boy became the greatest threat to Henry VII's throne. He led two military invasions of England. Both failed. In 1497, he was captured, locked in the Tower of London, and given a choice: confess or die.

He confessed. His name, he said, was Perkin Warbeck. His father was a merchant. Everything—the resemblance, the court knowledge, the royal backing—all of it was elaborate fraud.

Henry VII got what he needed. A signed confession. Public proof the threat was fake.

But we don't know if he was telling the truth.

In 1499, on November 23, he was hanged at Tyburn. Five days later, Edward Plantagenet, Earl of Warwick—a legitimate York heir who had been imprisoned since Henry VII took the throne in 1485—was beheaded.

You don't execute two rival heirs in the same week unless you're absolutely certain neither one is a threat. Unless they're both disposable.

Which raises a question Henry VII's confession never answered: Was Warbeck actually a fraud? Or was he the last living witness to what happened in the Tower?

To this day, historians can't agree. The resemblance to Edward IV was too close. The court knowledge too specific. But they can't prove he was real. No DNA. No verification.

He died claiming to be someone else. History recorded his confession. And the mystery of who he really was died with him at Tyburn, 1499.

Three men had motive to kill the princes. One of them might have been the prince himself, tortured into denying it. We'll never know which story is true.

But here's what we do know.

[CH13 | 21:15–21:35 | cliffhanger_pivot]

Three suspects. Three possible motives. Three chains of evidence that don't add up the same way.

One ordered the murder from inside the Tower. One knew it had already happened. One needed it to happen to secure his throne.

Before we close this, we need to look at what the actual evidence says about each of them.

[CH14 | 21:35–23:50 | crime_reconstruction]

Based on the public record—the testimony, the timing, the forensic gaps—here's the suspect list.

Suspect one: Richard III. Motive: his nephews stood between him and the crown. In June 1483, Parliament declared their father's marriage invalid. The boys lost their inheritance. Richard took the throne.

Evidence: the boys vanished while in his custody. Mancini recorded them disappearing under his watch. His own supporters turned against him. The Duke of Buckingham, who helped him seize power, rebelled three months later. Historians believe Buckingham already knew the princes were dead.

Weakness: there is no contemporary evidence Richard ordered it. The detailed murder narrative—Tyrrell, the smothering, the burial under the stairs—all written after Richard died. Written by the regime that replaced him. The Croyland Chronicle says only that there were rumors. Robert Ricart's record says the boys were "put to silence." No confession. No witness. No direct accusation while Richard was alive. Every complete account came from Tudor sources.

Suspect two: Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham. Motive: he had royal blood. He was in the line of succession himself.

Evidence: Philippe de Commines, writing in France, named Buckingham directly. In October 1483, Buckingham suddenly turned against Richard and launched a rebellion. Historians note the timing—he acted as if he already knew the princes were dead.

Weakness: Buckingham was executed in November 1483. Two months after the rebellion. Whatever he knew died with him. No trial record survives.

Suspect three: Henry VII. Motive: he seized the throne by force in 1485. The princes, if alive, were the same threat to him Richard faced.

Evidence: Tyrrell's so-called confession only appears in Tudor-era texts. Thomas More's account, written under Henry VIII thirty years after the princes vanished, gives Tyrrell the blame. In 1499, Henry VII had the Earl of Warwick executed. Warwick was another Yorkist heir, imprisoned for fourteen years since 1485. The pattern is clear: Henry eliminated rival claimants.

Weakness: there's no evidence the princes were still alive in 1485 when Henry won at Bosworth. If they died in 1483, Henry couldn't have killed them. But he could have shaped the narrative. The confession document itself has never been found.

Three motives. Three moments when murder made political sense. But the contemporary record gives us rumors and silence. The complete story only appears decades later, written by the winners.

The 1674 skeletons fit More's description of the burial site. But More also said the bodies were moved. And the staircase where the bones were found might not have existed in 1483.

The Windsor coffins remain unopened. The Westminster remains have never been tested.

Three suspects. All with motive. All with circumstantial links. Not one tied to the crime by forensic evidence or a reliable contemporary witness.

Which brings us back to the question that started this. Not who killed the princes—but why, ninety years after we had the technology to answer it, no one has been allowed to ask the bones.

[CH15 | 23:50–24:35 | killer_unmasking_downfall]

Here's what this five-hundred-year mystery actually reveals. Not who killed the princes—but why three institutions chose not to find out.

In 2012, when Richard III's skeleton was found under a parking lot in Leicester, scientists ran a full DNA analysis. They matched mitochondrial DNA from his maternal descendants. They published their findings in peer-reviewed journals. They gave him a state funeral.

The whole process was transparent, publicly funded, and celebrated as a triumph of modern forensic science applied to medieval history.

The princes' bones, sitting in Westminster Abbey, have never received that same treatment.

Same timeframe. Same technology. Same five-hundred-year gap.

One set of remains—the accused killer—got the full scientific validation.

The other set—the victims—has been locked behind a refusal that spans three generations of petitioners, two monarchs, and ninety years of available evidence.

And it's not just Westminster. In 1789, workers found two more child-sized coffins in Windsor, in the same chapel where the princes' parents are buried. Identity unknown. Never opened. Still there.

Two bone containers in Westminster. Two nameless coffins in Windsor. The technology to answer both questions. And a refusal that no institution will explain.

The more revealing question is why every institution with authority over the remains has declined to test them, even after Richard III’s DNA identification showed what such testing can establish: the Crown, the Church, and the academic establishment.

DNA could tell us if those bones are the princes. It can't tell us who killed them. And that's exactly the problem.

Because once you confirm the bones, you reopen every political and historical narrative built on their uncertain fate. You force a reckoning with five centuries of propaganda, legitimacy claims, and carefully managed ambiguity.

The urn remains closed because the institutions responsible have decided that reopening it carries a cost they are unwilling to pay. That decision, not the limits of science, keeps the mystery intact.

[CH16 | 24:35–25:00 | verdict_closure_cta]

Science can tell you if those bones belong to two young princes who vanished in 1483.

It cannot tell you who put them there.

The bones are still there. The chicken bones are still mixed in. The technology is still available. The only thing missing is permission.

Even if the lab confirms their identity beyond doubt, you still don't know if it was an uncle, a rival, or someone else entirely. The bones answer one question. They don't answer the other.

And maybe that's why three institutions—the Royal Family, Westminster Abbey, and five centuries of historians—have all chosen the same thing: to leave the mystery intact.

Thanks for watching. What would you do if you were on the decision panel in 2013? Drop your answer below. And if you think the bones should be tested, there are active petitions—links in the description. And if you want more unsolved cases where the evidence is there but the answers stay locked away, check out our playlist on historical mysteries that refuse to close.

Next time someone says "history has the answer," ask: did they test it, or did they just decide it?

We'll see you next time.
